SOLUTION: I wrote a server called Gypsy that essentially completely prevents such attacks and their consequences by simply not allowing any new connection for a client IP address which already has X active client-server connections. What happens is that clients (e.g., browsers) are greedy; they want for their one client up to 10 or more connections with a server, to "simultaneously" download web page elements (text, images, etc). Just code the server to limit any client's number of active connections to X, where, say, X is 2, 3 or 4 only. This also works quite well if the attacker has activated a number of "slave clients" (e.g., other computers infected with malware controlled by the attacker) to "magnify" the attack. One can add code to reject any new connections from a particular IP address for a set number of minutes if specific "too greedy" criteria are met. This latter anti-attack option must take into account that all browsers I have seen are greedy and will attempt to make an essentially unlimited number of simultaneous connections to get a web page's elements all loaded and displayed for non-hacking, ordinary users.

This above anti-DoS code is easy to write and use in servers. Why is it not used more often by server operators? Probably because they want their site to be "attractive" in terms of fast loading into client browsers. However, at some point, say, for VOAT, such code to "limit greedy access" by individual IP addresses might be considered and implemented.

SUMMARY: the server simply maintains in real-time a list of all connected IPs and the current number of open connections for each. If the number of presently open for an IP is greater than a preset number, incoming connection requests from that IP address receive NO response. At the client level, these connection request packets time out. The key is that a connection typically requires RAM and other resources on the server side. My solution above prevents excessive server resource use by "greedy" or attacking clients.

Agreed. At the network/hardware-interface level, code could reject/ignore incoming client connect packets per the criteria I described. My Gypsy server provides easy, total control of open sockets (as other servers can do also). When number of allowed connections from one client IP is exceeded, incoming resource requests have two results: 1. the socket is immediately closed (with client automatically so notified) and 2. as a consequence, that resource request is not honored. Yes, the packets to connect or make requests are a much smaller part of bandwidth usage (server RAM, CPU usage, etc) compared with honoring requests (e.g., a single request might require transfer to the client of many kilobytes or megabytes of content).
